summary.text: Letting \(m=D(n)\), the congruence \(n\equiv m\pmod 9\) gives \(n=m+9y\); choose \(x\equiv-y\pmod m\), and use eventual periodicity of \(10^r\bmod m\) to construct a sparse decimal number \(K\) with \(n-x\) suitably spaced 1’s and another \(x\) shifted 1’s, so that \(D(K)=n\) and \(K\equiv 10^L(n+9x)=0\pmod m\). Taking \(L\ge n\) ensures \(K>n\), hence \(K\) is a positive distinct partner.

full_proof.text:
Let \(D(r)\) denote the sum of the base-10 digits of the nonnegative integer \(r\). We prove that every positive integer \(n\) has a positive Harshad amicable partner distinct from itself. It will then follow immediately that the least such partner, which is \(a(n)\), is nonzero.

Fix \(n>0\), and put
\[
 m=D(n).
\]
We will use two standard facts about decimal digit sums:

1. \(D(n)>0\) when \(n>0\).
2. \(D(n)\le n\), and \(D(n)\equiv n\pmod 9\).

For completeness, the positivity in (1) follows because a decimal expansion whose digit sum is zero has every digit equal to zero and therefore represents zero. The inequality in (2) is the usual digit-sum bound: if \(n=\sum_i d_i10^i\), then \(D(n)=\sum_i d_i\le \sum_i d_i10^i=n\). The congruence follows from \(10^i\equiv1\pmod9\).

Thus
\[
 0<m\le n.
\]
Moreover, since \(n\equiv m\pmod9\) and \(m\le n\), there is a nonnegative integer \(y\) such that
\[
 n=m+9y. \tag{1}
\]
Explicitly, \(y=(n-m)/9\).

We next choose a nonnegative integer \(x\) satisfying
\[
 x\le n \quad\hbox{and}\quad m\mid x+y. \tag{2}
\]
Such a choice can be made by taking the least nonnegative residue of \(-y\) modulo \(m\):
\[
 x=(m-(y\bmod m))\bmod m.
\]
Then \(0\le x<m\le n\), and \(x+y\equiv0\pmod m\), proving (2). Define
\[
 c=n-x.
\]
Since \(x\le n\), this is a nonnegative integer and
\[
 c+x=n. \tag{3}
\]
In particular, \(c\le n\), \(x\le n\), and because \(n>0\), at least one of \(c,x\) is positive.

We also need an eventual repetition among the powers of \(10\) modulo \(m\), with the repetition beginning sufficiently far out.

Consider first the \(m+1\) residues
\[
 10^m,10^{m+1},\ldots,10^{2m}\pmod m.
\]
There are only \(m\) residue classes modulo \(m\), so two of these are equal. Consequently there are integers \(L_0\ge m\) and \(P>0\) such that
\[
 10^{L_0}\equiv10^{L_0+P}\pmod m. \tag{4}
\]
Multiplying (4) successively by powers of \(10^P\) shows, by induction on \(q\ge0\), that
\[
 10^{L_0}\equiv10^{L_0+qP}\pmod m. \tag{5}
\]
We may therefore move the starting exponent as far to the right as desired. In particular, set \(L=L_0+nP\). Then \(L\ge n\), and applying (5) with \(q=n\) and \(q=n+1\) gives
\[
 10^L\equiv10^{L+P}\pmod m. \tag{6}
\]
It follows more generally from (6), again by induction, that for every \(q\ge0\),
\[
 10^{L+qP}\equiv10^L\pmod m. \tag{7}
\]
Multiplying this congruence by \(10\) also gives
\[
 10^{L+qP+1}\equiv10^{L+1}\pmod m. \tag{8}
\]

We now construct the desired partner \(K\) directly through its decimal digits. For each \(j=0,1,\ldots,n-1\), place a digit \(1\) in decimal position \(L+2Pj\) if \(j<c\), and place a digit \(1\) in position \(L+2Pj+1\) if \(j<x\). Put zero in all other positions. Thus
\[
 K=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}
 \left(
  \mathbf 1_{j<c}\,10^{L+2Pj}
  +\mathbf 1_{j<x}\,10^{L+2Pj+1}
 \right), \tag{9}
\]
where \(\mathbf 1_E\) is \(1\) if \(E\) holds and \(0\) otherwise.

This really is a decimal expansion with no carrying. Indeed, \(P>0\), so each interval of positions
\[
 L+2Pj,\ L+2Pj+1,\ldots,L+2P(j+1)-1
\]
is a block of length \(2P\). In its first two positions we put the indicated zeros or ones, and all its remaining positions are zero. Distinct blocks occupy disjoint positions. Hence every displayed coefficient is an actual decimal digit, equal to either zero or one.

There are exactly \(c\) ones of the first kind, because among \(0,\ldots,n-1\) exactly \(c\) indices satisfy \(j<c\); here we use \(c\le n\). Similarly, there are exactly \(x\) ones of the second kind. It follows from (3) that
\[
 D(K)=c+x=n. \tag{10}
\]
Leading or trailing zeros in the finite description do not affect this digit sum.

We next prove that \(m=D(n)\) divides \(K\). In (7) and (8), take \(q=2j\). Then for every \(j\ge0\),
\[
 10^{L+2Pj}\equiv10^L\pmod m,
 \qquad
 10^{L+2Pj+1}\equiv10^{L+1}\pmod m.
\]
Reducing (9) term by term modulo \(m\), we therefore obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
 K
 &\equiv \sum_{j=0}^{n-1}
 \left(\mathbf 1_{j<c}10^L+\mathbf 1_{j<x}10^{L+1}\right)\pmod m\\
 &=c10^L+x10^{L+1}\pmod m\\
 &=10^L(c+10x)\pmod m.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(c=n-x\), we have \(c+10x=n+9x\). Using (1),
\[
 n+9x=m+9(x+y).
\]
But \(m\mid x+y\) by (2), so \(m\mid m+9(x+y)\). Consequently
\[
 K\equiv10^L\bigl(m+9(x+y)\bigr)\equiv0\pmod m.
\]
Thus
\[
 D(n)=m\mid K. \tag{11}
\]

It remains to ensure that \(K\) is positive and distinct from \(n\). In fact, the construction makes \(K>n\). Because \(c+x=n>0\), either \(c>0\) or \(x>0\). If \(c>0\), the term for \(j=0\) includes \(10^L\). If \(c=0\), then \(x=n>0\), and the term for \(j=0\) includes \(10^{L+1}\). All terms in (9) are nonnegative, so in either case
\[
 K\ge10^L.
\]
For every nonnegative integer \(r\), one has \(10^r>r\): this is immediate for \(r=0\), and if \(10^r>r\), then \(10^{r+1}=10\cdot10^r>r+1\). Since \(L\ge n\), it follows that
\[
 K\ge10^L\ge10^n>n. \tag{12}
\]
Thus \(K>0\) and \(K\ne n\).

Finally, (10) says \(D(K)=n\), and hence
\[
 D(K)\mid n. \tag{13}
\]
Combining (11), (12), and (13), \(K\) is a positive integer distinct from \(n\) such that
\[
 D(n)\mid K
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 D(K)\mid n.
\]
Therefore \(K\) is a Harshad amicable partner of \(n\).

We have shown that the set
\[
 S_n=\{k\in\mathbb N:k>0,\ k\ne n,\ D(n)\mid k,\ D(k)\mid n\}
\]
is nonempty for every \(n>0\). By the well-ordering principle it has a least element. Every member of \(S_n\), including its least element, is positive. By the definition of the sequence, when this set is nonempty, \(a(n)\) is precisely that least element (and the fallback value \(0\) is used only when the set is empty). Hence \(a(n)>0\), and in particular
\[
 \boxed{a(n)\ne0}
\]
for every positive integer \(n\).
